reference.source: Swaiman's Pediatric Neurology / Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies
clinicalPearls: The prototypical monogenic type I interferonopathy, presenting as an inflammatory encephalopathy that mimics congenital (TORCH) infection but without an identifiable pathogen
Caused by mutations in genes handling nucleic acids, including TREX1, the RNASEH2 subunits, SAMHD1, ADAR1 and IFIH1, with both recessive and dominant forms
Typical features are early developmental regression, acquired microcephaly, dystonia, irritability and unexplained fevers
Neuroimaging classically shows intracranial (basal ganglia) calcification, white matter abnormalities and cerebral atrophy
Cerebrospinal fluid characteristically shows a chronic lymphocytosis and raised interferon-alpha, with a peripheral interferon signature on gene-expression testing
Chilblain-like acral skin lesions are a recognised extraneurological manifestation
Management is supportive with emerging use of interferon-pathway-directed therapy such as JAK inhibition to dampen the interferon response
reference.pathophysiology: Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome is a genetically determined type I interferonopathy in which defects in intracellular nucleic-acid metabolism cause self-derived DNA and RNA to accumulate or to be misrecognised as foreign. The causative genes encode nucleases and nucleic-acid-editing or sensing proteins (for example the exonuclease TREX1, the ribonuclease H2 complex, the deoxynucleotide-regulating enzyme SAMHD1, the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, and the cytosolic RNA sensor encoded by IFIH1). When these fail, endogenous nucleic acids trigger innate immune sensors and drive chronic overproduction of type I interferon. Sustained interferon signalling produces the inflammatory encephalopathy, intracranial calcification, white matter injury and systemic features that characterise the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital infections (cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, herpes, Zika)
Other type I interferonopathies (e.g. STING-associated vasculopathy, proteasome-associated syndromes)
Mitochondrial and other inborn metabolic encephalopathies
Cerebral folate deficiency and other causes of intracranial calcification
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood interferon signature (interferon-stimulated gene expression)
Cerebrospinal fluid interferon-alpha and lymphocyte count
Neuroimaging (CT for calcification, MRI for white matter and atrophy)
Comprehensive genetic testing of the AGS-associated genes
Exclusion of congenital infection with appropriate serology and molecular testing
Skin examination and biopsy of chilblain lesions where present
redFlags: Rapid neurological regression and loss of acquired milestones
Progressive acquired microcephaly and worsening dystonia
Features initially mistaken for congenital infection but with negative pathogen workup
Systemic inflammation, cytopenias or evidence of overlapping autoimmunity
reference.prognosis: The classic early-onset form often causes severe, permanent neurological disability with significant early mortality, though a wide clinical spectrum exists including milder later-onset presentations; interferon-directed therapies offer the prospect of attenuating disease activity, particularly the systemic and skin manifestations.
pitfalls: Persistently pursuing a congenital infection when repeated pathogen testing is negative
Overlooking the interferon signature and cerebrospinal fluid findings that point to an interferonopathy
Attributing basal ganglia calcification solely to prior infection or metabolic causes
Failing to consider genetic counselling given both recessive and dominant inheritance patterns
management: Consider Janus kinase inhibition such as baricitinib to dampen type I interferon signalling and attenuate disease activity
Treat seizures, dystonia and irritability symptomatically with antiseizure and antispasticity medication
Provide nutritional support, often by gastrostomy feeding, and manage swallowing and respiratory difficulties
Manage chilblain-like acral skin lesions with warmth, skin protection and vasodilatory measures
Deliver developmental therapies, tone management and specialist neurodisability care
Monitor for complications including glaucoma, hypothyroidism and intracranial vascular disease
Offer genetic counselling and testing of the causative genes TREX1, RNASEH2, SAMHD1, ADAR1 and IFIH1 for recurrence risk and prenatal options
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through clinical immunology, neurology and paediatrics
